extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty, department chairs, curriculum designers, and administrators responsible for undergraduate quantitative literacy (QL) programs
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, implementing, and assessing undergraduate quantitative literacy programs and courses (placement, foundations courses, infusion courses, advising, and faculty development) at colleges and universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Quantitative Literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Quantitative literacy (QL) can be described as the ability to adequately use elementary mathematical tools to interpret and manipulate quantitative data and ideas that arise in individuals’ private, civic, and work lives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes numeracy (understanding of numbers and magnitude); some geometric, algebraic and algorithmic skills; problem solving ability; understanding of probability and statistics; and the ability to quickly capture information, summarize it, and make a decision. QL is a 'habit of mind' best formed by exposure in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program responsiveness to local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any specific quantitative literacy program must be responsive to the local conditions of an institution including its mission, its student clientele, its history and its resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design should adapt to institutional mission and student population; expected proficiency levels and program form can legitimately vary by institutional mission and type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tiered program structure (foundations + infusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The core of the program is a two-tiered system consisting of a 'foundations' course usually taken during the first or second year and 'infusion' or applied courses taken in the latter years of undergraduate study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations courses develop core skills (often offered by math departments). Infusion/applied courses are offered by disciplines outside mathematics and use those foundational skills to address context-relevant problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate placement exam
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete quantitative literacy program would include an appropriate placement exam so that students are able to move efficiently to a course in which they will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement helps route students to remedial, foundational, or directly to applied courses as appropriate; placement decisions should be backed by advising and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial component for underprepared students
rubrics_metrics.description: The program may very well have a remedial component for those students who are not prepared for the collegiate level work being offered at their institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remediation can be part of the foundations tier or separate, and is necessary because many incoming students lack mastery of core QL skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus core mathematical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a consensus on the mathematical skills necessary to be quantitatively literate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skills explicitly listed include elementary logic; the basic mathematics of financial interest; descriptive statistics; finite probability; an elementary understanding of rates of change; ability to model problems with linear and exponential models; estimation and approximation; and general problem solving. Programs should explicitly address these areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-centered pedagogy and active engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to be actively engaged in their learning experience by reading, writing, working in groups, collecting and manipulating data, and interpreting answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy should favor active, student-centered methods rather than passive lecture; assignments and assessments should require doing and interpreting real quantitative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and connectivity across the curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is an integrated experience; each course should be connected to others either formally in the curriculum or through explicit recognition that material in one course can be used in other courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QL is reinforced when courses are coordinated or when faculty acknowledge cross-course use of quantitative tools; infusion into non-math disciplines supports this integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial time and energy are required to prepare faculty (including TAs and part-time instructors) to include QL topics in their courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should plan for training, support, and possibly incentives for faculty across departments to teach QL materials effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for articulated standards of mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: A very significant gap in the literature is an articulated statement of standards for what 'mastery' means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should attempt to define concrete mastery standards and align courses and assessments to those standards; absence of clear targets undermines assessment and claims of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment practices and program evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should address assessment of QL and describe assessment practices, placement, advising, and remediation as part of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must be built into program planning (e.g., measuring whether students achieve listed skills), and practice examples are provided in several essays in the volume; assessment should inform placement, remediation, and curricular changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of course types for QL outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all mathematics courses equally advance QL; e.g., traditional college algebra often does not develop QL, while calculus, statistics, or finite mathematics are generally assumed to, though evidence is not always provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course designers should evaluate whether a course's content and pedagogy develop the target QL skills (courses emphasizing 'great ideas' or mathematical beauty may not sufficiently build practical QL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement of other departments (infusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics departments should assist colleagues in other disciplines to infuse appropriate QL experiences into their courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdepartmental collaboration expands contexts for QL, places QL work in disciplinary relevance, and helps form the 'habit of mind' across the curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement, advising, and student resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective placement, advising, and student resources are key elements of QL programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advising models (decentralized/centralized/shared) affect implementation; advisor training, printed/web guides, decision trees, and online tools can improve course selection and student success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program model should fit institution size and type
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach to addressing students' quantitative literacy depends significantly on the size and type of institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller liberal-arts schools tend toward infusion-based models; mid-sized schools use quantitative courses across and outside math; large schools often rely heavily on the mathematics department. Choose a model compatible with available resources and mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and sequencing of QL experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations courses should occur early (first/second year), and infusion/applied courses should come in later undergraduate years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early grounding plus repeated application in later courses supports the development of QL as a habit of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation management and realistic goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should set realistic expectations for what all college graduates can attain in QL given diversity of students; institutions should define concrete, local competence expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National diversity makes a universal single standard impractical; institutions are advised to define 'reasonable proficiency' concretely for their context and make demonstration of proficiency a degree requirement where appropriate.
